subject: sociology
book: Indian Society; Social Change and Development in India (NCERT, rationalised)

sections.name: 1.1 Introducing Indian Society: Unlearning and Self-reflexivity

concepts.text: Note: this chapter is non-evaluative in the CBSE 2026-27 syllabus
Students already have common-sense knowledge of Indian society, gained through socialisation
Sociology asks us to unlearn taken-for-granted ideas and look at society freshly
Self-reflexivity: seeing ourselves as others see us and questioning our own position
Sociology as a kind of social map that locates the individual in a wider social landscape
Colonialism as the context in which modern Indian society and Indian self-awareness took shape
Colonial rule unified India administratively and economically, but through exploitation
Colonial economic, political and administrative changes (railways, law, land revenue, education)
Paradox: colonialism produced the forces that opposed it, including Western-educated nationalists
Nationalism and the idea of India as a nation formed through anti-colonial struggle
Communities (caste, tribe, religion, region) and classes (new middle class, workers, peasants) emerging and organising
Reform and revival movements reshaping community identity
Overview of later chapters: demography, institutions (caste, tribe, family), inequality and exclusion, cultural diversity, project work
Explain self-reflexivity and why it matters in studying one's own society
Discuss how colonialism shaped Indian society and nationalism

chapters.title: Indian Society: The Demographic Structure of the Indian Society

concepts.text: Demography: systematic study of population - size, composition, distribution and change
Formal demography (mathematical measurement) versus social demography (population studies of social causes and effects)
Demography grew with the modern nation-state and statistics; census as a key source
History of the census in India: first attempts 1867-72, regular decennial census since 1881; post-independence censuses
Rates as social facts, e.g. Durkheim on suicide rates

sections.name: 2.2 Some Theories and Concepts in Demography

concepts.text: Malthusian theory: population grows geometrically, food supply arithmetically
Malthus' positive checks (famine, disease, war) and preventive checks (late marriage, celibacy, abstinence)
Criticisms of Malthus: Europe's history disproved him; technology raised food output; liberal and Marxist critics blamed unequal distribution, not population
Theory of demographic transition: population growth linked to economic development
Three stages: high birth and death rates with low growth; falling death rate with high birth rate (population explosion); low birth and death rates with low growth
Why death rates fall faster than birth rates (medicine, sanitation versus slow change in social attitudes)
Birth rate: live births per 1000 population per year
Death rate: deaths per 1000 population per year
Rate of natural increase (growth rate) = birth rate minus death rate; replacement level when near zero
Fertility rate: births per 1000 women of child-bearing age (15-49)
Total fertility rate: average number of children a woman would bear; replacement TFR about 2.1
Infant mortality rate: deaths of infants under one year per 1000 live births
Maternal mortality rate: deaths of women in childbirth per 100,000 live births
Life expectancy: estimated average years a person is expected to live
Sex ratio: number of females per 1000 males
Age structure of the population and age pyramids
Dependency ratio: dependants (under 15 and over 64) relative to working-age population (15-64)
Demographic dividend: benefit from a large working-age share, but only if jobs and education are provided
Population momentum: population keeps growing even after fertility falls

sections.name: 2.3 The Size and Growth of India's Population

concepts.text: India's population growth from 1901 to 2011; slow growth before 1921
Negative growth in 1911-21 due to the influenza epidemic of 1918-19
Rapid growth after 1921 and especially 1951-81 as death rates fell sharply
Causes of falling death rates: control of famines and epidemics (plague, smallpox, cholera), vaccination, sanitation
Famines caused by poverty, low food output, poor transport and state inaction; Amartya Sen's 'failure of entitlements'
Famine prevention and rural employment schemes (e.g. MGNREGA)
Birth rate falls slowly because it is socio-culturally rooted
Regional variation in fertility: low TFR states (Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Punjab etc.) versus high TFR states (Bihar, UP, MP, Rajasthan)
Data-reading type: interpret tables and charts of population, growth rates and birth/death rates

sections.name: 2.4 The Age Structure of the Indian Population

concepts.text: India's young population and the changing shares of 0-14, 15-59 and 60+ age groups
Age pyramids over time and differences between states (e.g. Kerala versus Uttar Pradesh)
Falling dependency ratio as an opportunity (demographic dividend) and its conditions
Problems of rising unemployment among youth and ageing populations

sections.name: 2.5 The Declining Sex Ratio in India

concepts.text: Historical decline in India's sex ratio through the 20th century
Child sex ratio (0-6 years) falling faster than the overall ratio
Reasons: son preference, neglect of girl children, female infanticide and sex-selective abortion
Lowest child sex ratios in prosperous regions, showing prosperity alone does not remove bias
Legal response: PCPNDT Act (1994, amended 2003) banning sex determination; schemes like Beti Bachao Beti Padhao
Long-term solution requires change in social attitudes
Literacy as a means of empowerment and as an influence on health and fertility
Rise in literacy from 1951 to 2011 and the gender gap in literacy
Inequalities in literacy by region (e.g. Kerala versus Bihar) and by social group (SC/ST)
Most Indians still live in villages, but the urban share is rising
Declining share of agriculture in GDP while many still depend on it
Push factors for migration: lack of rural work, decline of common property resources, need for cash
Pull factors: urban jobs and anonymity, which can free lower castes from rural caste oppression
Mass media and communication bringing urban lifestyles to villages
India launched a national family planning programme in 1952, among the first in the world
Objectives: influence the rate and pattern of population growth through birth control and health measures
Emergency period (1975-76): coercive mass sterilisation and the resulting backlash
Renaming as National Family Welfare Programme and a non-coercive approach
National Population Policy 2000 and National Health Policy 2017 goals (TFR 2.1, lower infant/maternal mortality)
Lesson: the state can create conditions, but fertility change follows social and economic change
Explain the basic argument of the theory of demographic transition and the link between transition and population explosion
Why was Malthus wrong? Evaluate his theory
Explain why mortality fell while birth rates stayed high
Which states are near or below replacement fertility and which have high growth; give reasons
What is the age structure and why is it relevant; explain the demographic dividend
What is the sex ratio, and what explains its decline
Read population tables and charts and draw conclusions

chapters.title: Indian Society: Social Institutions: Continuity and Change

concepts.text: Caste, tribe and family as key institutions of Indian society that show both continuity and change
Caste as a European-derived word (casta) for the Indian terms varna and jati
Varna: fourfold classification (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) plus those outside it (ati-shudra/untouchables)
Jati: local, regionally variable groups that are the real units of caste
Caste in the past: ancient origins, changing over time; rigidity increased in later periods
Features of caste: membership by birth, endogamy, food and commensality rules, hierarchy, segmental sub-divisions, hereditary occupation
Two organising principles: difference/separation and wholeness/hierarchy based on purity and pollution
Caste and economic/political power: caste rank and material status usually coincided
Colonialism and caste: colonial attempts to classify and count caste in the census (1901 census under Risley ranking castes)
Colonial land revenue settlements gave upper castes legal property rights
Government of India Act 1935 creating schedules of castes and tribes for state welfare
Caste in the present: nationalist and reform opposition to caste (Phule, Ambedkar, Gandhi)
Contradiction: the independent state wanted to abolish caste but used caste for reservations
Industrialisation, urbanisation and education weakening caste rules in public life (jobs, food, travel)
Persistence of caste in the cultural and domestic sphere, especially endogamy
Caste in politics: caste associations, vote banks and political mobilisation
Dominant castes (M.N. Srinivas): numerically large, landowning, politically strong middle castes after land reforms
Sanskritisation as a route of caste mobility
Caste made 'invisible' for urban upper castes, who benefited from it, but hyper-visible for SC/ST/OBC who depend on caste-based claims
'Tribe' as a modern administrative and colonial category; tribes as communities outside the caste-Hindu fold
Classification by permanent traits: region, language, physical/racial features and ecological habitat
Regional concentration: North-East, central India, and smaller groups elsewhere
Language families of tribes: Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Austric and Tibeto-Burman
Physical-racial categories once used: Negrito, Australoid, Mongoloid, Dravidian, Aryan
Size of tribes: from millions (Gonds, Bhils, Santhals) to very small groups in the Andaman Islands; tribals about 8 per cent of population
Classification by acquired traits: mode of livelihood (fishers, hunter-gatherers, shifting cultivators, peasants, plantation and industrial workers)
Classification by extent of incorporation into Hindu society
Debate on the concept of tribe: tribes were not isolated or 'primitive'; many were secondary formations shaped by contact with states
Historical evidence: Gond kingdoms, tribal chiefdoms, trade and military roles
Isolation versus integration debate (protectionists like Elwin versus integrationists like Ghurye)
National development versus tribal development: dams, mines, industries and forest policy causing displacement
Tribal identity today: forced incorporation into mainstream, resistance and assertion
Statehood for Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh; continuing problems
Special laws in the North-East limiting civil liberties and cycles of rebellion and repression
Emergence of an educated tribal middle class through reservation and its effect on identity
Two key issues in tribal movements: control over resources (land, forests) and ethnic-cultural identity
Nuclear family (couple and unmarried children) versus extended/joint family
Debate on whether India had mainly joint families; nuclear families always existed in some groups
Diverse forms by residence: matrilocal and patrilocal
By succession/inheritance: matrilineal and patrilineal
By authority: matriarchal and patriarchal
Changes in family structure: accidental (war, migration) or deliberate; grandparents' new roles in urban families
Changes in marriage: love marriages, changing age at marriage, resistance to inter-caste marriage
Matrilineal societies: Khasi (Meghalaya) and Nair (Kerala)
Khasi matriliny: property passes from mother to daughter but control rests with maternal uncle; role strain for men
Matriliny versus matriarchy: inheritance through women is not the same as women holding power; matriarchy remains theoretical
Gender and family: son preference and patriarchal norms
Explain the role of colonialism in shaping caste
Why has caste become 'invisible' for the urban upper castes?
Describe the two principles of caste: separation and hierarchy
Discuss the debate on whether tribes are primitive and isolated; describe tribal classification
What are the main issues behind tribal movements today?
Describe diverse family forms and explain matriliny versus matriarchy with the Khasi example

chapters.title: Indian Society: Patterns of Social Inequality and Exclusion

concepts.text: Institutions such as caste, tribe, family and market also produce inequality and exclusion
Inequality often appears natural or deserved, leading people to blame the poor
Group-based differences, not just individual talent or luck, explain most social inequality
Activity type: compare a typical day of rich and poor people by interviewing workers of different levels

sections.name: 4.2 What is Social about Social Inequality and Exclusion?

concepts.text: Three senses in which inequality is social: it is about groups, it is not only economic, and it is systematic and structured
Social inequality: unequal distribution of valued resources (money, property, education, health, power)
Pierre Bourdieu's three forms of capital: economic, cultural and social; they can be converted into one another
Social stratification: ranking of categories of people in a hierarchy that shapes life chances
Principle 1: stratification is a feature of society, not individual difference; it arises with surplus production
Principle 2: stratification persists over generations through inheritance and ascribed status (caste, endogamy)
Principle 3: stratification is supported by beliefs or ideology (e.g. purity and pollution)
Prejudice: pre-formed opinions about a group, not based on evidence, resistant to change; can be positive or negative
Stereotypes: fixed images of a group (e.g. colonial 'martial races'), ignoring individual variation
Discrimination: actual behaviour denying a group opportunities; often hidden and justified as 'merit'
Social exclusion: being cut off from full participation in society and services (health, banking, police, education)
Exclusion is involuntary and structural; it can lead the excluded to stop trying to participate
Law alone cannot end prejudice; sustained social campaigns are needed
Transgender and third gender identities and their legal recognition
Activity type: analyse prejudiced portrayals of groups in films or novels

sections.name: 4.3 Caste and Tribe: Systems Justifying and Perpetuating Inequality

concepts.text: Caste as a system that legitimises discrimination: humiliating, exclusionary and exploitative
Ideal of separating ritual and economic status versus the practical overlap of caste and class
Weakening caste-occupation link since the 19th century, but caste-class correlation remains strong at the macro level
Data-reading type: poverty (2011-12) and affluence tables by caste and religion, rural and urban
Comparison box: race and apartheid in South Africa, the ANC struggle and Nelson Mandela
Untouchability: extreme caste practice against those considered polluting; pan-Indian with regional forms
Three dimensions of untouchability: exclusion, humiliation-subordination and exploitation
Practices: denial of water sources, temple entry, ceremonies; 'distance pollution' in parts of the south
Names: Gandhi's term 'Harijan' and the self-chosen term 'Dalit' (oppressed), popularised by the Dalit Panthers
State initiatives: scheduled lists from 1935; reservations in legislatures, government jobs and education
Laws: Caste Disabilities Removal Act 1850, Article 17 abolishing untouchability, SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989, 93rd Amendment 2005 for OBC reservation in higher education
Non-state initiatives: Dalit movements and leaders (Phule, Periyar, Iyothee Thass, Ambedkar), Dalit parties and Dalit literature
Other Backward Classes: castes with low status but above untouchability, mainly service and artisan castes
Constitutional idea of 'socially and educationally backward classes'; OBCs exist in non-Hindu religions too
Backward Classes Commissions: Kaka Kalelkar (1953) and B.P. Mandal (implemented 1990)
Earlier backward class movements and policies in southern states
Internal divide among OBCs: landed dominant upper OBCs versus poor lower OBCs
Poem 'The City' (Daya Pawar) on persisting caste in a modern age
Adivasi struggles: poverty, powerlessness and stigma of Scheduled Tribes
Colonial forest policy turning adivasis into 'encroachers'; loss of shifting cultivation and gathering rights
Displacement by mines, dams and industries after independence (e.g. Sardar Sarovar, Polavaram) without fair compensation
Liberalisation easing corporate land acquisition in tribal areas
The term 'adivasi' (original inhabitants) as a political assertion; 'diku' meaning outsiders
Achievements: statehood for Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh; adivasis were concentrated in contiguous areas unlike Dalits
Activity type: list constitutional articles and laws relating to SC/ST and untouchability

sections.name: 4.4 The Struggle for Women's Equality and Rights

concepts.text: Gender inequality is social, not natural; evidence from matrilineal societies (Nairs, Khasis) and women farmers/traders in Africa
The women's question arose in 19th-century middle-class reform movements
Raja Rammohun Roy's campaign against sati; Brahmo Samaj
M.G. Ranade on widow remarriage using scriptures and Western moral philosophy
Jyotiba Phule's attack on caste and gender oppression; Satyashodhak Samaj
Sir Syed Ahmed Khan and Muslim reform; girls' education at home; Dayanand Saraswati's similar approach
Tarabai Shinde's 'Stree Purush Tulana' (1882) protesting double standards for men and women
Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain's 'Sultana's Dream' (1905): a role-reversed utopia and early science fiction
Women's organisations of the early 20th century and women in the national movement
Karachi Congress resolution (1931) on fundamental rights and equality of women
Revival of the women's movement in the 1970s; legal reform campaigns in the 1980s
New challenges such as the declining child sex ratio
Activity types: study a local reformer; list jobs open and closed to women; group project on reservation or domestic violence
Disability as a social, not only biological, condition: society is built to exclude impaired people
Anita Ghai on the invisibility of disabled people
Common perceptions: disability as biological, the disabled as victims, as dependent, linked to self-perception
Derogatory terms and the 'bechara' attitude; impairment seen as fate or karma in culture and myth
Newer terms like 'differently abled' and 'visually impaired' replacing insulting labels
Social barriers: inaccessible buildings, courts and schools; segregated schooling debates
Close link between poverty and disability, each worsening the other
Census 2011 approach to counting disability (eight types)
Laws: Persons with Disabilities Act 1995 and later rights-based legislation
Activity types: study folklore portrayals of disability; discuss films like 'Iqbal'
How is social inequality different from individual inequality?
Describe the features of social stratification
Distinguish prejudice from other opinions; define stereotypes and discrimination
What is social exclusion?
What is the relationship between caste and economic inequality today?
What is untouchability, and what policies address caste inequality?
How are OBCs different from Dalits?
What are the main issues of adivasi struggles today?
What major issues has the women's movement taken up over time?
Explain why disability is as much social as physical

chapters.title: Indian Society: The Challenges of Cultural Diversity

concepts.text: Cultural diversity: differences of language, religion, sect, race or caste rather than inequality
Why diversity is challenging: identities arouse passions; diversity overlaps with inequality; scarce resources (river water, jobs, funds) fuel conflict
India as one of the most culturally diverse nations
Community identity is ascriptive: based on birth and belonging, not on achievement
Membership is unconditional and hard to escape; others may still identify us by it
Socialisation and significant others; mother tongue as a carrier of culture
Community ties give security and meaning, so threats provoke strong reactions
Conflicts over identity are hard to resolve as each side sees the other as a mirror-image enemy
Nation: a large community of communities, easy to describe but hard to define
State: political-legal institutions claiming control of a territory and a monopoly of legitimate force (Weber)
Nation-state: a nation with its own state; no fixed relation between nation and its communities
Examples: Soviet nationalities, diasporas, dual citizenship
States seek legitimacy from 'the people' and the nation
States suspicious of diversity try to suppress it through assimilation or integration policies
Assimilation: forcing minorities to adopt the dominant culture; integration: keeping minority culture private
Typical homogenising measures: centralised power, one language, dominant symbols and holidays, seizing minority lands
Such suppression is costly and backfires; recognising diversity is wiser

sections.name: 5.4 Cultural Diversity and the Indian Nation-State

concepts.text: India's diversity in numbers: population, many languages, 22 scheduled languages, religious composition (Census 2011)
Distribution of religious minorities across states
India's 'state-nation' model: unity with diversity; multiple complementary identities
Constitution as secular but not banishing religion or language from public life
India follows neither assimilation nor integration; problems lie in implementation
Regionalism rooted in geographically concentrated language, culture, tribe and religion, plus regional deprivation
Reorganisation of multilingual presidencies into linguistic states; States Reorganisation Commission (1956)
Potti Sriramulu's fast and the formation of Andhra Pradesh
Linguistic states strengthened national unity (contrast with Sri Lanka's Sinhala-only policy and Pakistan's split)
New states in 2000 (Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand) formed on tribal identity, deprivation and ecology
Federalism as accommodation: Union, State and Concurrent lists; Rajya Sabha; Finance Commission; GST Council
Activity type: research how your state was formed and current demands for new states

sections.name: 5.6 The Nation-State and Religion-related Issues and Identities: Minority Rights and Nation Building

concepts.text: Inclusive, democratic nationalism; Gandhi and Tagore's critiques of exclusive nationalism
Sociological meaning of minority: small number plus disadvantage and group solidarity
Privileged minorities (e.g. Parsis, Sikhs) can still face cultural disadvantage
Ambedkar's argument for protecting minorities to keep the nation united
Articles 29 and 30: right to conserve culture and to establish minority educational institutions
Forced imposition of a dominant culture weakens national unity (Bangladesh 1971, Sri Lanka)
Communalism: aggressive political ideology based on religious identity, distinct from personal piety
Communalism treats religious identity as overriding and religious groups as homogeneous
History of communal riots: colonial divide-and-rule, pre-colonial conflicts and post-independence violence
Traditions of pluralism and syncretism: Bhakti and Sufi movements, Kabir
Western secularism: separation of church and state, linked to rationality and modernity
Indian secularism: equal respect for all religions, the opposite of communalism
Tension between protecting minorities and accusations of 'appeasement' or vote-bank politics
Activity type: collect stories and songs of religious harmony from elders
Authoritarian state: no voice for people, rulers not accountable; civil liberties at risk
Emergency (1975-77) as a lesson on the value of civil liberties
Civil society: non-state, non-market public sphere of voluntary associations (parties, media, unions, NGOs, religious groups)
Issues taken up by civil society: tribal land rights, anti-violence campaigns, displacement, slum rights, education
Right to Information Act 2005: origin in a Rajasthan grassroots campaign; provisions and impact
Activity type: identify civil society organisations near you and compare them with government and commercial bodies
What is cultural diversity, and why is India very diverse?
What is community identity and how is it formed?
Why is the nation hard to define; how are nation and state related?
Why are states suspicious of cultural diversity?
What is regionalism; has linguistic reorganisation helped or harmed India?
What is a minority and why do minorities need protection?
What is communalism; what are the senses of secularism in India?
What is the relevance of civil society organisations today?

chapters.title: Indian Society: Suggestions for Project Work

concepts.text: Note: this chapter is non-evaluative in the CBSE 2026-27 syllabus; it supports the 20-mark project
Purpose: give students first-hand experience of doing small sociological research
The research question determines the method; there is no single best method
Surveys and questionnaires for collecting information from many people
Interviews: structured and open-ended conversations
Participant and non-participant observation
Use of archives, old documents, photographs and media as sources
Combining methods (mixed methods) for a fuller picture
Ethics: consent, privacy and respect for respondents

sections.name: 6.3 Possible Themes and Subjects for Small Research Projects

concepts.text: Public use of space: who uses streets, parks, bus stops and how
Media: changes in newspapers or television content over time
Households and domestic work: division of labour within homes
Transport: modes of travel and their social aspects
Life histories of people, places or everyday objects
Other locally chosen themes related to the book's chapters
Project components: introduction, statement of purpose, research question, methodology, data analysis, conclusion
Viva voce based on the project
Colonialism's contradictory impact on modern India: liberal ideas under illiberal rule
Chapter focus on two structural changes - industrialisation and urbanisation - in colonial and independent India
Everyday colonial legacies: parliamentary, legal and police systems, schools, driving on the left, English as advantage and privilege
Colonialism: rule of one country over another; modern colonialism far more transformative than earlier conquests
Pre-capitalist empires took tribute; capitalist colonialism restructured the economic base of the colony
Colonial interventions in land ownership, crops, forests and labour
Colonialism moved people: labour migration to Assam tea gardens and plantations abroad (indenture to Mauritius, Fiji, Caribbean)
Movement of the middle classes and professionals within India
Western education creating a new middle class that became a source of nationalist consciousness
Capitalism: economic system based on private ownership and profit, with origins in exploration, plunder and science
Link between Western capitalism and colonialism
Nation-state as a modern political form; nationalism and the demand for self-rule (swaraj)
Indian nationalists exposed the contradiction of British liberal claims and colonial rule

sections.name: 7.4 Industrialisation and Urbanisation: The Colonial Experience

concepts.text: Industrialisation: rise of machine production using non-human power; usually linked with urbanisation
Britain: rapid shift of population to cities with industrialisation
India: deindustrialisation - decline of artisanal manufacture and old towns (Surat, Masulipatnam) and loss of court towns
Workers pushed back into agriculture; growth of a weak colonial middle class
Census of 1911 evidence on village artisans abandoning crafts

sections.name: 7.5 Colonial Cities: Links between Core and Periphery

concepts.text: Coastal colonial cities (Bombay, Calcutta, Madras) as links between colony (periphery) and Britain (core)
Colonial cities as concrete expression of global capitalism; exporting raw materials (cotton, jute, indigo)
Calcutta's growth from three villages leased by the East India Company; Fort William
Divided colonial city: separate European 'white town' and native 'black town'
Activity type: trace the renaming of colonial cities

sections.name: 7.6 The Tea Plantations: Colonial Industry and Coerced Labour

concepts.text: Tea industry in Assam from the 1850s and its huge labour needs
Recruitment of labourers by fraud and coercion; harsh working conditions
Colonial laws backing planters, e.g. the Transport of Native Labourers Act 1863 and amendments
Contrast between planters' lavish life and labourers' misery
Economic exploitation as a central nationalist grievance; Swadeshi
Industrialisation as the path to growth and social justice after independence
Planned development: heavy industry, public sector and mixed economy
New industrial townships (Bhilai, Bokaro, Rourkela, Durgapur)
Cooperative models such as Amul and Operation Flood
Rapid urban growth after independence; urban share rising from about 17 per cent (1951) to about 31 per cent (2011)
M.S.A. Rao's three situations of urban impact on villages
Situation 1: villages sending migrants to distant cities and receiving remittances
Situation 2: villages near a new industrial town, e.g. Bhilai
Situation 3: villages swallowed by a growing metropolis
Data-reading type: urban population, number of towns and growth rates 1951-2011
Urbanism as a way of life (Louis Wirth)
How has colonialism affected our lives?
Industrialisation and urbanisation are linked: discuss with British and colonial Indian experience
Write the history and present status of a town or city you know
Is your place a village, town or city? Give sociological reasons
Cultural change through deliberate reform movements and through less deliberate processes
Four processes: Sanskritisation (pre-colonial origins), Westernisation, Modernisation and Secularisation
Tradition is living and is reinterpreted; colonial modernity was paradoxical

sections.name: 8.2 Social Reform Movements in the 19th and Early 20th Century

concepts.text: Issues targeted: sati, child marriage, ban on widow remarriage, caste discrimination, women's education
Earlier challenges to discrimination by Buddhism, Bhakti and Sufi movements; the new feature was the modern context
Satish Saberwal's three aspects of modern change: new modes of communication, new forms of organisation, new nature of ideas
Modes of communication: printing press, telegraph, railways, steamships
Forms of organisation: Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj, All-India Muslim Ladies Conference, newspapers and journals
Ideas: Western liberalism mixed with new readings of tradition
Raja Rammohun Roy using natural rights and scriptures against sati
M.G. Ranade on scriptural sanction for widow remarriage; Vidyasagar's writing on widow remarriage
Sir Syed Ahmed Khan's interpretation of Islam (ijtihad) compatible with science
Kandukuri Viresalingam's use of classical Indian logic for reform
Jyotiba Phule's first girls' school in Pune and claim of a pre-Aryan golden age
Differences within reform: upper-caste versus Dalit concerns; Dalit rejection of Hinduism; Jahanara Shah Nawaz's resolution against polygamy
Orthodox opposition groups such as the Dharma Sabha
Activity type: study a reformer such as Pandita Ramabai, Sri Narayana Guru or Dayanand Saraswati

sections.name: 8.3 How Do We Understand the Different Kinds of Social Change?

concepts.text: The four processes overlap and vary by region; a person can be modern in some ways and traditional in others
Colonial modernity involved reinterpreting tradition, e.g. the sari with blouse and petticoat
Definition (M.N. Srinivas): a lower caste, tribe or group adopts the rituals, customs and lifestyle of a higher (dwija) caste
Regional variation: dominant castes set the cultural model; de-Sanskritisation where non-Sanskritic castes dominate
Preconditions: improved economic or political position, or contact with the 'Great Tradition'
Resistance by dominant castes; Kumud Pawade's experience
Criticisms: exaggerates mobility (positional not structural change); accepts upper-caste superiority
Criticisms: justifies inequality and purity-pollution; harms women (seclusion, dowry replacing bride-price); erodes Dalit culture and dignity of labour
Backward class movements and Dalit assertion as alternatives to Sanskritisation
Definition (Srinivas): changes in Indian society and culture from over 150 years of British rule in technology, institutions, ideology and values
Kinds: a westernised sub-culture of early elites, and a general spread of Western traits (dress, food, technology)
Adopting Western forms does not necessarily bring democratic or egalitarian values
Western influence on art and literature: Raja Ravi Varma, Abanindranath Tagore, Chandu Menon, Bankimchandra
Debate on whether upper castes westernise and lower castes Sanskritise; case of the Thiyyas of Kerala
Generational conflicts over Western dress and lifestyle
Modernisation: first about technology and production, later the Western path of development

Rudolph and Rudolph's features of modernity: universal over local ties, utility and science over the sacred, individual as unit, choice over birth, achievement over ascription, work separate from home
Limits in India: caste-based occupations, endogamy and religion persist alongside modern institutions
Secularisation: declining influence of religion (Western sense)
Secular dimensions of rituals: displays of wealth and status, socialising (e.g. weddings)
Secularisation of caste: caste moving from purity-pollution to political pressure groups, caste associations and parties
Rajni Kothari: caste changes under politics as politics is shaped by caste
Colonialism produced unintended, paradoxical cultural changes
Ideas of equality and democracy led to reinterpretation of tradition
Write a critical essay on Sanskritisation
Is westernisation only about adopting Western dress and lifestyle? Explain
Write a note on rites and secularisation
Write on caste and secularisation
Explain how Sanskritisation affects women and gender

chapters.title: Social Change: Change and Development in Rural Society

concepts.text: Agriculture is the main livelihood of rural India and shapes its culture and festivals (Pongal, Bihu, Baisakhi, Ugadi)
Rural society is more than agriculture: artisans, service castes and non-farm work

sections.name: 9.2 Agrarian Structure: Caste and Class in Rural India

concepts.text: Agrarian structure: distribution of land ownership shaping rural class relations
Classes: large landowners, middle and small farmers, tenants, landless agricultural labourers
Strong overlap of caste and land: dominant landowning castes (e.g. Jats, Patidars, Reddis, Kammas, Vokkaligas, Marathas)
Most agricultural labourers belong to Dalit and lower castes
Women's limited land rights despite heavy farm work
Traditional dependency relations: jajmani system, bonded labour (e.g. Halpati in Gujarat, begar)
Colonial land revenue systems: zamindari and ryotwari and their effects
Land reform aims after independence: reduce inequality and raise productivity
Abolition of the zamindari system removing intermediaries
Tenancy abolition and regulation laws giving tenants security
Land ceiling acts limiting holdings and redistributing surplus land
Limited success: evasion through benami transfers, splitting land among relatives, eviction of tenants
Regional variation in success (more effective in Kerala and West Bengal)

sections.name: 9.4 The Green Revolution and its Social Consequences

concepts.text: Green Revolution: HYV seeds, fertilisers, pesticides and irrigation from the 1960s in Punjab, western UP, coastal Andhra and Tamil Nadu
First phase benefits mainly for medium and large landowners; rising productivity
Displacement of tenants and service castes; mechanisation reducing labour demand
Growing regional inequality between Green Revolution and other areas
Commercialisation of agriculture and market dependence
Second phase spreading to dry and rain-fed areas; ecological costs (soil, water)

sections.name: 9.5 Transformations in Rural Society after Independence

concepts.text: Shift from patronage-based to contractual, cash-wage labour relations
Rise of capitalist farming and a new rural entrepreneurial class
Dominant castes investing in education, business and politics
Decline of traditional bonds and of the jajmani system
Seasonal migration of agricultural labourers to prosperous regions and cities
Jan Breman's 'footloose labour': migrants moving without job security
Preference for migrant labour as cheaper and easier to control
Feminisation of agricultural labour as men migrate
Liberalisation exposing Indian agriculture to world markets
Contract farming: companies dictate crops and buy produce; risks for farmers
Entry of multinational agribusiness in seeds, fertilisers and pesticides
Loss of local knowledge and biodiversity; dependence on corporate inputs
Agrarian distress and farmer suicides: debt, crop failure, falling prices and lack of support
Explain the agrarian structure and its link with caste
What were the land reform measures and why did they have limited success?
Discuss the social consequences of the Green Revolution
Describe changes in rural labour relations and the circulation of labour
Explain the effects of globalisation on agriculture; why do farmers commit suicide?

chapters.title: Social Change: Change and Development in Industrial Society

concepts.text: Classical sociologists on industry: Marx on alienation of workers from their product and labour
Assembly line and repetitive work (image of Charlie Chaplin's 'Modern Times')
Industrialisation bringing equality in some respects (trains, offices) and new inequalities
Scientific management (Taylorism) and Fordist mass production
Indian pattern differs from the West: most workers still in agriculture and the unorganised sector
Organised (formal) sector versus unorganised (informal) sector and their differences in job security and benefits
Early years of independent India: public sector and planned industrial development
Globalisation and liberalisation: disinvestment, privatisation, outsourcing and contract work
Effects of liberalisation on employment security and the growth of informal work
Self-employment and casual work for most Indians
Employment exchanges and formal recruitment for a few
Role of contractors, jobbers and mistris recruiting workers, often from their own village or caste
Social networks of kin and caste in getting jobs; badli (substitute) workers
Managers aim to control workers and raise output
Methods: lengthening the working day or increasing speed of work; assembly lines setting the pace
Example of a car factory: tight shifts, short breaks and high stress
White-collar and IT work: long hours, deadlines and 'flexible' time
Hazardous conditions in mines, quarries and factories; laws like the Mines Act and their poor enforcement
Contract workers in mines and construction lacking safety and benefits
Accidents, occupational diseases and lack of compensation
Home-based work: production done at home for traders or firms (e.g. bidi rolling, agarbatti, papad, embroidery)
Mostly women and children, paid on piece rates, with no job security
Strike: workers stop work to press demands; lockouts by management
Rise of trade unions in India and their role in protecting workers
Bombay textile strike of 1982 and its impact on mill workers
Weakening of unions with informalisation and liberalisation
Compare work in the organised and unorganised sectors
How do people find jobs? Discuss the role of contractors and networks
Describe working conditions in mines or factories and home-based work
How has liberalisation affected employment patterns?
Discuss strikes and unions with an example
Social movements have shaped modern rights and institutions (e.g. labour laws, women's rights)
Movements as collective attempts to bring about or resist change
Sustained collective action over time, not a one-off protest
Shared objectives and ideology among participants
Some organisation, leadership and decision-making structure
Counter-movements arise to defend the status quo (e.g. Dharma Sabha against the anti-sati campaign)
Methods of protest: marches, dharnas, hunger strikes, petitions, songs and poetry
Early sociologists saw movements as threats to social order; later ones as sources of change
Theory of relative deprivation: conflict arises when groups feel worse off than others
Limits of relative deprivation theory: grievances alone do not cause movements
Mancur Olson's 'Logic of Collective Action': rational individuals join only if gains exceed costs
Resource mobilisation theory (McCarthy and Zald): success depends on mobilising leadership, resources and networks
Critique: movements can succeed even with limited resources
Redemptive movements aim to change individuals' inner consciousness (e.g. Narayana Guru's Ezhava movement)
Reformist movements aim to change social and political arrangements step by step
Revolutionary movements aim to transform society radically, often by seizing state power
'Old' social movements: class-based, worked through political parties (working-class, anti-colonial)
'New' social movements: about quality of life, environment, identity and rights, often outside parties
Old and new movements overlap in India; issues of identity and of resources are often combined
Development's costs to nature and people: deforestation, dams and displacement
Chipko movement in the Himalayas: villagers hugging trees to protect forests
Chipko combined ecological, economic (subsistence) and political (local control, against the state) concerns
Ecological movements question the dominant model of development
Peasant movements in colonial India: Bengal indigo revolt, Deccan riots, Champaran (1917), Bardoli (1928)
Formation of the All India Kisan Sabha (1936)
Post-war peasant struggles: Tebhaga (Bengal), Telangana and Naxalbari
New farmers' movements from the 1970s (Punjab, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra): issues of prices, inputs and subsidies; non-party organisation
Workers' movements: early strikes in mills, Madras Labour Union (1918), AITUC (1920)
Splits in unions along party lines; decline of unions with the informal sector
Railway strike (1974) and other major workers' struggles
Dalit movement: struggle for dignity, equality and self-respect, not just economic gains
Examples: Satnami movement, Adi-Dharma movement in Punjab, Mahar movement in Maharashtra, Ambedkar's leadership
Dalit Panthers and Dalit literature as forms of assertion
Backward class and caste movements, especially in the south (non-Brahmin movements)
Trends in upper caste responses: perceived 'reverse discrimination' and anti-reservation protests
Tribal movements largely in central India 'tribal belt' and the North-East
Jharkhand movement: long struggle against dikus (outsiders), moneylenders and land loss; led to the state of Jharkhand (2000)
Birsa Munda's revolt as a symbol of tribal resistance
Issues: land alienation, forest rights, displacement by mining and dams, cultural identity
North-East movements: ethnic identity, autonomy and land rights
Early 20th-century women's organisations: Women's India Association (1917), All India Women's Conference (1926), National Council of Women in India
Women's participation in the freedom struggle and in peasant and tribal movements (e.g. Tebhaga, Telangana)
Revival in the 1970s: 'Towards Equality' report (1974) and new autonomous women's groups
Campaigns against custodial rape (Mathura case), dowry deaths and violence; legal reforms
Shift of focus from 'welfare' to 'rights' and 'empowerment'; issues of diverse women (Dalit, tribal, working)

Compare relative deprivation, collective action and resource mobilisation theories
Distinguish redemptive, reformist and revolutionary movements; old and new social movements
Explain why the Chipko movement is an ecological and economic movement
Compare peasant and new farmers' movements; trace the workers' movement
Discuss the Dalit and tribal movements; describe phases of the women's movement
